questions.problem:
The inverse of the matrix $N$ is found using row operations, as shown below. What are the row operations corresponding to the blank spaces?

$$
\begin{aligned}[N\,|\,I] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & ↔{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -2 & 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \text{___________} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \text{___________} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{1}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We write down $N$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply the standard Gauss-Jordan method to transform the matrix $N$ into the identity matrix. We perform the same row operations on both matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}[N\,|\,I] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & ↔{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -2 & 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{1}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding row operations are

$$
{R}_{1}↔\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2},\,{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1},\,{R}_{2}:=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2}.
$$

The matrix ${N}^{-1}$ is given by the right-hand side of our big matrix after all of the transformations have been completed. Therefore, 

$$
{N}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ \frac{1}{2} & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following first-order linear differential equations are homogeneous?

I. ${y}^{′}+7xy=5$

II. ${y}^{′}+7xy=0$

III. ${y}^{′}+7xy=-2y$
questions.worked_solution:
A first-order linear differential equation is homogeneous if it can be written in the form

$$
{y}^{′}+P(x)y=0.
$$

Now, let's consider each equation in turn.

- First, we consider the equation

$$
{y}^{′}+7xy=5.
$$

The presence of the constant term $5$ means the right-hand side is not zero, and so it cannot be rewritten in homogeneous form. Thus, this equation is *not* homogeneous.

- Next, we consider the equation

$$
{y}^{′}+7xy=0.
$$

The right-hand side is already zero, so the equation directly matches the form ${y}^{′}+P(x)y=0.$ Therefore, this equation is homogeneous.

- Finally, we consider the equation

$$
{y}^{′}+7xy=-2y.
$$

We move the term involving $y$ to the left side so that all $y$-terms are together:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}+7xy & =-2y \\ {y}^{′}+7xy+2y & =0 \\ {y}^{′}+(7x+2)y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This matches the homogeneous form ${y}^{′}+P(x)y=0.$  Therefore, this equation *is* homogeneous.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

questions.problem:
The matrix form of the affine transformation

$$
x=6u+4v+2,\,y=5v-1
$$

is shown below. What is the value of $a+b+c?$

$$
[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}6 & a \\ 0 & b\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2 \\ c\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

First, notice that we can express the given transformation as

$$
[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}6u+4v+2 \\ 5v-1\end{aligned}].
$$

Separating the constants and expressing the linear part as a product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}6u+4v+2 \\ 5v-1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6u+4v \\ 5v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}6 & 4 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=4+5+(-1)=8.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the straight line given by the following parametric equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=t-2 \\ y=2-3t \\ z=2t-1\end{aligned}
$$

Find a vector that is parallel to the line.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's find the corresponding vector equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}t-2 \\ 2-3t \\ 2t-1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}t \\ -3t \\ 2t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ r & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ \,2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$ 

This implies that the straight line passes through the point $(-2,2,-1)$  and is parallel to the vector $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

questions.worked_solution:
The product rule for double summations states that

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{a}_{i}{b}_{j}={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{a}_{i}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{b}_{j}.
$$

So, using the product rule for double summations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{5}{\sum }_{j=1}^{20}({a}_{i}+1)({b}_{j}-1) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{5}({a}_{i}+1){\sum }_{j=1}^{20}({b}_{j}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the rules for single summations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{5}({a}_{i}+1){\sum }_{j=1}^{20}({b}_{j}-1) & =({\sum }_{i=1}^{5}{a}_{i}+{\sum }_{i=1}^{5}1)\cdot ({\sum }_{j=1}^{20}{b}_{j}-{\sum }_{j=1}^{20}1) \\  & =(20+5)\cdot (26-20) \\  & =(25)\cdot (6) \\  & =150.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\int \frac{8}{|x|\sqrt{8{x}^{2}-1}}\text{d}x=\int \frac{8\sqrt{8}}{|\sqrt{8}x|\sqrt{(\sqrt{8}x)^{2}-1}}\text{d}x.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\text{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $\sqrt{8}x.$

So, let's substitute $u=\sqrt{8}x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt{8}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{8}}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{8}{|x|\sqrt{8{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{8\sqrt{8}}{|\sqrt{8}x|\sqrt{(\sqrt{8}x)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =8\sqrt{8}\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{8}}\text{d}u) \\  & =8\sqrt{8}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{8}}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =8\,\text{arcsec }u+C \\  & =8\,\text{arcsec}(\sqrt{8}x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the unit tangent vector to the curve $r(t)=⟨-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩$ at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{3}.$
questions.worked_solution:
For a curve $r(t)=⟨x(t),y(t),z(t)⟩$, the unit tangent vector $T(t)$ at the point $P(x(t),y(t),z(t))$ is given by

$$
T(t)=\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}.
$$

First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=\frac{\pi }{3}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{3}) & =⟨\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}),\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}),\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3}{2},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{3}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{3})‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}+{(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})}^{2}+(1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{9}{4}+\frac{3}{4}+1} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{3})$ and obtain the unit tangent vector to the given curve at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{3}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(\frac{\pi }{3}) & =\frac{{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{3})}{‖{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{3})‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}⟨\frac{3}{2},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},1⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3}{4},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4},\frac{1}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following matrices are symmetric?

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -3 & -2 \\ 1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}],\,Q=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}],\,R=[\begin{aligned}5 & 8 \\ 8 & -5\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
A square matrix $A$ is symmetric if it is equal to its transpose:

$$
A={A}^{T}
$$

Equivalently, ${a}_{ij}={a}_{ji}$ for all $i,j.$ In other words, $A$ is symmetric across its main diagonal. 

With that in mind, let's examine each matrix in turn.

- $P$ is a symmetric matrix. Indeed, $P={P}^{T}.$

- $Q$ is *not* a symmetric matrix. Since ${q}_{12}\ne {q}_{21},$ we obtain $Q\ne {Q}^{T}.$

$$
Q=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

- $R$ is a symmetric matrix. Indeed, $R={R}^{T}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$P$ and $R$ only."
